title: Empresses, Armies and a Dangerous Gamble
summary: In the 1700s, inoculation spread from rich families in London to an empress in Russia and a whole army in America. It saved many lives, but it was still a risky gamble that could make people very sick. Even a famous mathematician tried to work out, with numbers, whether the gamble was worth it.

sections.heading: Inoculation Goes on the Road
paragraphs: After the excitement of 1721 and 1722, you might expect inoculation to have swept through Britain like wildfire. It did not. For about twenty years it grew only slowly. A few wealthy families used it, but the deaths that sometimes followed, and the fear of starting new outbreaks, kept many people away. Doctors argued about it in pamphlets, and clergymen argued about it in sermons.

In the American colonies, however, epidemics kept forcing people to make a choice. In 1738, when smallpox struck Charleston in South Carolina, a doctor named John Kirkpatrick reported that about 800 people had been inoculated there and only about eight of them had died, around 1 in 100. In a town where natural smallpox was killing far more, numbers like that were hard to ignore.

By the 1740s and 1750s inoculation was becoming more common in Britain. In 1746 a charity hospital opened in London especially for smallpox and inoculation, so that poorer people could be treated too. And across the country, inoculators set up 'inoculation houses': buildings, often outside towns, where people came to be inoculated and then stayed, cut off from their neighbours, until they were no longer infectious. A stay could last two weeks to a month or more.

The operation itself was quick. The inoculator dipped the point of a small, sharp blade called a lancet into fluid or matter from a smallpox sore on someone with a mild case, then made a small scratch or cut on the patient's arm and placed the material inside. For about a week the patient usually felt fine, and the spot on the arm grew red and swollen. Then came a fever, headache and aching back, followed by a crop of spots, often far fewer than in natural smallpox and clustered near the scratch. After two or three weeks the scabs dropped off. Before going home, patients were usually washed, and their clothes were cleaned or aired, because people knew the scabs could still pass on the disease.

What happened inside these houses could be grim. Doctors of the time believed that a person had to be 'prepared' for inoculation to make the illness milder. Preparation often meant weeks of a special, very plain diet without meat, doses of medicines to make people vomit or empty their bowels (called 'purging'), and bleeding, which meant cutting a vein to let out some blood. We now know that none of this helped. In fact, bleeding and starving people probably weakened them.

We have a vivid example. In 1757 an eight-year-old boy in Gloucestershire went through this kind of preparation. He was bled repeatedly and given very little to eat for weeks before his inoculation, and he remembered the experience for the rest of his life. Recovery took about a month. His name was Edward Jenner, and you will meet him again soon.

Then came a family of inoculators who changed the business. Robert Sutton, a surgeon in Suffolk in eastern England, began offering what he advertised as a 'new method' of inoculating in the late 1750s and 1760s. He and his sons, especially Daniel Sutton, made only a tiny, shallow scratch instead of a deep cut, used material from people with mild cases, kept preparation short, and did not bleed their patients. They also encouraged patients to get fresh air during recovery. Their results were excellent, and they became famous and rich.

The Suttons kept their method secret, sharing it only within the family and with partners who paid to use it, a little like a modern franchise. By 1770 the Sutton family and their partners are said to have inoculated more than 300,000 people. Daniel Sutton finally explained the method in a book called 'The Inoculator' in 1796. Their simpler approach was safer and cheaper, and it helped inoculation spread to many more people, including whole villages that were sometimes inoculated together during an epidemic.

sections.heading: Benjamin Franklin's Sorrow
paragraphs: Some of the most powerful arguments for inoculation came not from doctors but from parents. One of them was Benjamin Franklin, the printer, writer and scientist from Philadelphia who would later help found the United States.

Franklin and his wife Deborah had a little son named Francis, nicknamed 'Franky', born on 20 October 1732. By every account he was a bright, much-loved child. In 1736 smallpox came to Philadelphia. Francis had been ill with a stomach complaint, and Franklin decided to wait until the boy was stronger before having him inoculated. But before that could happen, Francis caught smallpox naturally. He died on 21 November 1736, just after his fourth birthday.

Franklin's grief was made worse by rumours. Because he was known as a supporter of inoculation, some people in Philadelphia whispered that Francis had died from being inoculated. That would have been a gift to the opponents of the practice. So, heartbroken as he was, Franklin printed a notice in his own newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette, explaining that his son had not been inoculated but had caught the disease 'in the common way of infection'.

Many years later, in his famous autobiography, Franklin wrote that he had 'long regretted bitterly' that he had not given his son the protection of inoculation. He added that he was writing this for the sake of other parents, so that they would not face the same regret. The gravestone of little Francis in Philadelphia described him as 'the delight of all who knew him'.

Franklin turned his sorrow into action. He collected numbers on inoculation and death in Boston and Philadelphia, and he worked with doctors to make inoculation cheaper and easier. In 1759 he teamed up with the London physician William Heberden on a pamphlet that explained, in plain language, how parents could inoculate their own children at home without paying expensive doctors. Heberden paid to print copies to give away in America. The cost of inoculation, which could be several weeks of a working family's income, was one of the biggest barriers, and Franklin wanted to remove it.

Franklin's story is a reminder of how hard decisions about inoculation were in the 1700s. It was not a small, safe step. It meant deliberately giving a child a real disease, and sometimes that child died. Parents had to weigh a smaller risk now against a larger risk later, without knowing when or if smallpox would come.

sections.heading: The Empress and the Quaker Doctor
paragraphs: In the summer of 1768, an English doctor received an astonishing invitation. Catherine II, Empress of Russia, known to history as Catherine the Great, wanted him to come to St Petersburg and inoculate her.

The doctor was Thomas Dimsdale, born in 1712 in Essex, England, into a Quaker family. Quakers were a Christian group known for their plain dress and simple lives. Dimsdale had trained in London and worked for decades as a doctor in the town of Hertford. He was an expert in inoculation and used a gentle method similar to the Suttons'. In 1767 he published a book called 'The Present Method of Inoculating for the Small-Pox', which was popular enough to go through five editions in two years. News of the book reached Russia.

Catherine had good reasons to be worried. Smallpox was a terror in Russia, as everywhere in Europe. The young Russian emperor Peter II had died of it in 1730, at just 14 years old. Catherine had one son, Grand Duke Paul, born in 1754, the heir to the throne. If smallpox killed her or Paul, the empire could be thrown into chaos. Catherine was also proud of being a modern, scientific ruler who read the latest ideas from Western Europe, and she wanted to set an example for her people.

Dimsdale travelled to St Petersburg with his son Nathaniel, who was a medical student. He was nervous, and with good reason. If the empress died after he inoculated her, he could be blamed, and he had no idea how the Russian court might react. Before the operation, it was quietly arranged for relays of fresh horses to stand ready along the road out of Russia, so that the Dimsdales could escape quickly if things went wrong.

Dimsdale first tested his method on some young people in St Petersburg to find a healthy donor with a mild case. Then, in October 1768, he inoculated the 39-year-old empress, using material taken from a young boy, usually named as Alexander Markov, who had a mild case. According to the accounts, Catherine had herself inoculated quietly, without public fuss. She had a mild illness, recovered well, and was soon back at work. Her son Paul, aged 14, was inoculated shortly afterwards and also recovered.

Catherine celebrated the success loudly. Church services of thanksgiving were held, and the boy Alexander Markov was rewarded by being made a nobleman, with the extra surname 'Ospenny', from the Russian word for smallpox. Dimsdale was made a baron of the Russian Empire and, according to most accounts, given £10,000 (an enormous fortune at the time), £2,000 for his expenses and a yearly pension of £500. His son Nathaniel was also made a baron. More than 140 members of the Russian court followed the empress's example and were inoculated.

Catherine hoped her example would encourage ordinary Russians, and inoculation centres were opened in some Russian cities. Dimsdale later returned to Russia, in 1781, to inoculate Catherine's grandsons. Back in England, he became a banker and a Member of Parliament for Hertford. One of his patients there was Mai (sometimes called Omai), a young man from the Pacific island of Raiatea who had come to Britain on one of Captain Cook's ships.

sections.heading: Washington's Secret Order
paragraphs: George Washington knew smallpox personally. In 1751, when he was 19, he sailed to the island of Barbados in the Caribbean with his older half-brother Lawrence, who was ill with tuberculosis and hoped the warm climate would help. While there, George caught smallpox. He was sick for weeks but recovered, with a few faint scars on his face. From then on he was immune, which turned out to be very lucky for the future of his country.

Twenty-four years later, in 1775, the American Revolution began, and Washington became commander of the Continental Army, the army of the thirteen colonies fighting for independence from Britain. Smallpox quickly became one of his most dangerous enemies, deadlier in some months than British bullets.

Many British soldiers had grown up in crowded towns in Britain where smallpox was common, so a large share of them had already had it as children and were immune. Many American soldiers came from farms and small villages where smallpox was rare, so they had never had it. When thousands of these young men were packed together in camps, smallpox could spread fast.

The disaster came in the American attempt to capture Quebec in Canada in 1775 and 1776. During the long, freezing siege of Quebec City, smallpox swept through the American camp. By the end of March 1776, the American force had grown to nearly 3,000 men, but almost a quarter of them were too sick to fight, mostly because of smallpox. Some desperate soldiers tried to inoculate themselves secretly, scratching smallpox matter under their fingernails with pins or needles. That spread the disease even further. Weakened by sickness, the army was forced into a long, chaotic retreat.

Inoculation was risky for an army, because newly inoculated soldiers would be sick for weeks, and while they were sick they could spread smallpox to others. Earlier in the war, inoculating soldiers had actually been forbidden, because commanders feared it would spread the disease, and Washington had been cautious too. But by the winter of 1776 to 1777, he became convinced that smallpox might destroy the army if he did nothing.

In early 1777, while the army was in winter quarters at Morristown, New Jersey, Washington made his decision. In early February he wrote to Dr William Shippen Jr., one of the army's senior doctors, ordering that all soldiers who had not had smallpox should be inoculated. He explained that if the disease spread through the army in the natural way, with its usual violence, it could do more harm than the enemy.

The operation had to be done carefully and quietly. If the British learned that large parts of the American army were lying sick for weeks at a time, they might attack. So the inoculations were carried out in groups, in secret as far as possible, and new recruits were inoculated as they arrived, before they joined their units. Special houses and hospitals were used, including in Philadelphia, so that sick soldiers were kept away from healthy ones.

It worked. This is often described as the first mass inoculation of an entire army. Smallpox did not disappear from the war, but it never again crippled the Continental Army the way it had at Quebec. Washington's biographer Ron Chernow called the decision as important as any military measure Washington took during the war. Washington's own wife, Martha, had been inoculated in 1776, so the general knew from his family's experience that it could be done safely.

sections.heading: The Price of the Gamble
paragraphs: So why didn't everyone simply get inoculated? Because inoculation had real problems, and it is important to be honest about them.

First, there was the cost. A full inoculation, with weeks of preparation, the operation itself, and a stay in an inoculation house while recovering, could cost far more than a poor family earned in a month. Rich families could afford it; poor families often could not. Working people also could not easily stop working for several weeks, and servants or labourers might lose their jobs.

Second, there was the illness. Inoculation gave a person a real case of smallpox, usually mild but sometimes not. Most people had a fever and a few spots and recovered within two or three weeks. But roughly 1 or 2 in every 100 died. Even royal families were not safe. In 1783, Prince Octavius, a four-year-old son of King George III of Britain, died a few days after being inoculated. People at the time argued about whether the inoculation was to blame, but the loss hit his father very hard.

Third, and perhaps worst, inoculated people were contagious. They could pass the full, natural smallpox on to people around them who were not immune. If inoculated patients were not kept carefully apart, inoculation could actually start new outbreaks. In France, an epidemic in Paris in the 1760s was blamed on inoculation, and the authorities banned it within the city, so doctors moved their practices to the suburbs.

In some American towns, anger about this danger turned violent. People who lived near inoculation hospitals feared that the disease would escape into their streets. In the 1770s, crowds in places such as Marblehead, Massachusetts, protested against private inoculation hospitals, and in early 1774 one built on an island off Marblehead was burned down.

France offers a dramatic example of what refusing inoculation could cost. In 1774 King Louis XV died of smallpox. A few weeks later, the new king, Louis XVI, and his younger brothers were inoculated, a step that made inoculation much more popular in France. The French writer Voltaire had argued decades earlier that if the French had used inoculation like the English, thousands of lives would have been saved.

Every family in the 1700s that thought about inoculation was really doing a kind of risk calculation in their heads. They were comparing a small, immediate danger that they chose with a larger danger that might or might not come later. It was a gamble. And in the 1760s, one of the cleverest mathematicians in Europe decided to work out the odds properly.

sections.heading: Doing the Maths: Daniel Bernoulli
paragraphs: Daniel Bernoulli was born in 1700 in Groningen, in what is now the Netherlands, into a family of Swiss mathematicians from Basel so brilliant that historians have to number them to keep them apart. Today he is best known for 'Bernoulli's principle', which explains how the pressure in a moving fluid changes with its speed and helps explain how aeroplane wings work. But he had also trained as a doctor, and he was fascinated by probability, the mathematics of chance.

In 1760, Bernoulli presented a paper to the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris that asked a simple but powerful question: if everyone were inoculated at birth, how much longer would people live on average? To answer it, he built what many historians consider the first mathematical model of the spread and effects of an infectious disease.

Bernoulli needed some numbers to start with. Using the death records available to him, he made estimates. Roughly speaking, he assumed that each year about 1 in 8 people who had never had smallpox would catch it, and that about 1 in 8 of those who caught it would die. He also took into account that many children would die of other causes before smallpox ever reached them. Then he used equations to follow an imaginary group of babies through life, year by year, counting how many caught smallpox, how many died from it, and how many survived.

He ran the calculation twice: once for a world with smallpox as usual, and once for a world where smallpox had been removed as a cause of death by inoculation, after subtracting the small risk of the operation itself. His answer was that average life expectancy at birth would rise from about 26 years and 7 months to about 29 years and 9 months, a gain of roughly three years.

You can picture his method with a thought experiment. Imagine 1,000 babies all born in the same year. Bernoulli's numbers let him estimate, year by year, how many of them would still be alive, how many had already survived smallpox and were now safe, and how many were still at risk. Each year, some of those at risk caught smallpox and some of those died. Over a lifetime, his calculation suggested that smallpox would kill around one in every thirteen of the babies, a huge toll. In the second, imaginary world, those smallpox deaths disappeared, apart from the few caused by inoculation, and more of the 1,000 survived into adulthood, raising the average.

Three years might not sound like much. But remember that this is an average over everyone, including the many who would never have died of smallpox. For the families who did lose someone, it meant a whole lifetime. Bernoulli concluded that, for society as a whole, inoculation was clearly worth it, and he argued that governments should support it. His paper was published in full in 1766.

Not everyone agreed with how he framed the question. The French mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert raised a thoughtful objection. Bernoulli's sums were about averages, he pointed out, but a real parent is not an average. Asking someone to accept a small risk of their child dying next month, in exchange for a longer life expectancy decades later, is not the same as simply comparing two numbers. People naturally care more about a danger right in front of them. D'Alembert did not oppose inoculation, but he argued that the decision involved feelings and values as well as mathematics.

That debate, between what is best for a whole population and how one person weighs a risk, is still discussed by scientists, doctors and philosophers today. Bernoulli's paper is often celebrated as the beginning of mathematical epidemiology, the science of using numbers and models to understand how diseases spread and how to control them.

sections.heading: Rumours From the Cowshed
paragraphs: By the 1790s, inoculation had come a very long way from the nutshell of an old woman in Constantinople and the memory of an enslaved man in Boston. It had protected an empress and her heir, a revolutionary army, princes and princesses, and hundreds of thousands of ordinary people. It had led to some of the first uses of statistics in medicine and to the first mathematical model of a disease.

And yet it was still a dangerous gamble. It still meant giving people a real case of smallpox. It still killed some of them. It still cost too much for many families. And it could still start new outbreaks. What the world really needed was a way to get the protection of smallpox without ever having smallpox at all.

The answer would come not from a palace or a university, but from the farms of the English countryside. In dairies in counties such as Gloucestershire and Dorset, people who milked cows sometimes caught a mild disease from sores on the cows' udders. It was called cowpox, and it gave the milkers a few blisters on their hands and perhaps a slight fever. And among the milkmaids and farmers, a curious piece of country wisdom was whispered: those who had caught cowpox from the cows never seemed to catch smallpox.

deepDive: Daniel Bernoulli's 1760 analysis, read to the Paris Academy of Sciences and published in 1766, is often called the first mathematical model in epidemiology. He set up equations for a group of people born at the same time and tracked two kinds of people at each age: those who had never had smallpox and those who had survived it. Using rough estimates drawn from the Breslau life tables and medical reports, he assumed that each year about 1 in 8 susceptible people caught smallpox and that about 1 in 8 of them died. Removing smallpox as a cause of death while allowing for the small risk of inoculation raised life expectancy at birth from about 26 years 7 months to about 29 years 9 months. Modern epidemiologists who have re-examined the paper, such as Klaus Dietz and Hans Heesterbeek, praise its logic while noting its simplifications. Bernoulli assumed a constant risk of infection at every age, so he ignored the way smallpox came in epidemic waves, and he did not model the fact that inoculated people could infect others. Jean le Rond d'Alembert's critique raised a deeper question that still matters in public health: how should an individual weigh a small immediate risk against a larger but delayed and uncertain one? Historians also debate how much the death rate from inoculation really fell during the century. Early figures of around 2 percent dropped substantially with the Sutton and Dimsdale methods, which used shallow scratches, mild donor material and no bleeding. These gentler methods probably produced milder infections because less material entered the body, although doctors at the time could not explain why. Washington's 1777 decision has been studied too. Because inoculation could spread smallpox, the army had to manage it with quarantine and timing, an early example of disease control planned as part of military strategy.
funFact: When Catherine the Great was inoculated in 1768, the boy whose mild smallpox supplied the material, Alexander Markov, was made a nobleman and given the extra surname 'Ospenny', taken from the Russian word for smallpox.
